title.title: Integer multiplication below $n \log n$
title.subtitle: Claim: one multitape Turing machine multiplies $n$-bit integers in $O(n(\log n)^{1-\kappa})$, $\kappa = 2^{-182}$

plain: Multiplying huge numbers: the best method was thought to be final. This claims to shave a hair off it

beats.text: In 1971 Schönhage and Strassen conjectured that $n \log n$ is optimal
Harvey and van der Hoeven reached $O(n \log n)$ exactly, thought to be the end
The claimed saving, $(\log n)^{2^{-182}}$, is indistinguishable from 1 at any real size

steps: Pass mixed combinations of the data, not the data itself
One pass then costs a little less than before
Nest that step inside itself: the saving compounds

data.unit: each block: a slightly cheaper pass
data.label: a saving that grows with every level

before.label: Best known since 2021
before.note: Harvey–van der Hoeven, Annals of Mathematics

achievement.note: Refutes the $n \log n$ conjecture in its own model. GMP is safe

verify.detail: No Lean statement; the DFT family 130 reuses its phase network
verify.ourCheck: We did not referee the 73-page proof; nothing is machine-checked

voice.text: Since twenty twenty one, n log n steps was thought to be the end.
Mixed combinations of data make each pass cheaper, and the saving compounds.
Claimed: a hair below n log n.

sources.quote: Schonhage-Strassen (1971) O(n log n log log n) and their conjecture that n log n is optimal
Harvey-van der Hoeven (Annals of Math 2021) O(n log n)
multiplies two n-bit integers exactly in O(n (lg n)^{1-kappa}) worst-case time with kappa = 2^{-182}
